confidence_note: Very strong evidence: uniform refrain throughout 26 verses, clear lexical/thematic correspondences in matching panels, theological crescendo to cosmic/creation center, validated by multiple scholarly sources

elements.label: A
elements.summary: Triple call to thank/praise YHWH with titles (LORD, God of gods, Lord of lords)
elements.text_excerpt: הוֹדוּ לַיהוָה כִּי־טוֹב / Give thanks to the LORD for he is good

elements.label: B
elements.summary: Creation acts: wonders, heavens, earth, luminaries (sun, moon, stars)
elements.text_excerpt: לְעֹשֵׂה נִפְלָאוֹת גְּדֹלוֹת לְבַדּוֹ / to him who alone does great wonders

elements.label: C
elements.summary: Exodus deliverance: struck Egypt's firstborn, brought Israel out, divided Red Sea, overthrew Pharaoh
elements.text_excerpt: לְמַכֵּה מִצְרַיִם בִּבְכוֹרֵיהֶם / to him who struck down the firstborn of Egypt

elements.label: X
elements.summary: Central pivot: YHWH leads his people through the wilderness—the transitional act between redemption and conquest
elements.text_excerpt: לְמוֹלִיךְ עַמּוֹ בַּמִּדְבָּר / to him who led his people through the wilderness

elements.label: C'
elements.summary: Conquest fulfillment: struck great kings (Sihon, Og), gave land as inheritance to Israel his servant
elements.text_excerpt: לְמַכֵּה מְלָכִים גְּדֹלִים / to him who struck down great kings

elements.label: B'
elements.summary: Providential care: remembered us in our low estate, rescued from foes, gives food to all flesh
elements.text_excerpt: שֶׁבְּשִׁפְלֵנוּ זָכַר לָנוּ / who remembered us in our low estate

elements.label: A'
elements.summary: Concluding call to thank God of heaven, echoing opening call to praise
elements.text_excerpt: הוֹדוּ לְאֵל הַשָּׁמָיִם / Give thanks to the God of heaven

pivot.label: X
pivot.summary: The wilderness journey forms the theological hinge between Egypt's defeat (C) and Canaan's conquest (C'), representing Israel's identity formation under divine guidance
pivot.theological_weight: The wilderness is not merely geographical transition but theological transformation—where liberated slaves become covenant people. This single verse crystallizes Israel's entire liminal experience: dependent wholly on YHWH's leading (מוֹלִיךְ) through barrenness, prefiguring all subsequent exiles and returns. The pivot's placement emphasizes that redemption requires formation; God's people must journey through testing before inheriting promise.

correspondences.evidence: Inclusio formed by identical imperative הוֹדוּ 'give thanks' with divine titles framing entire psalm; A uses 'LORD/God of gods/Lord of lords' while A' uses 'God of heaven,' creating envelope structure

B describes cosmic creation (heavens, earth, luminaries) while B' describes providential sustenance (remembering, rescuing, feeding all flesh); both emphasize God's universal care—creative and preservative power; lexical link through זָכַר 'remember' motif

Striking lexical parallel: C uses לְמַכֵּה מִצְרַיִם 'to him who struck Egypt' (v.10) and C' uses לְמַכֵּה מְלָכִים גְּדֹלִים 'to him who struck great kings' (v.17); both panels focus on military defeat of Israel's enemies; both culminate in Israel's liberation/inheritance; C ends Egypt's power, C' establishes Israel's territorial claim

methodology_citations: Dorsey (Literary Structure of the OT, pp. 192-193) identifies concentric structures in Psalms based on refrain analysis and thematic correspondence. Lund (Chiasmus in the New Testament, 1942, pp. 40-41) establishes that refrains function as structural markers confirming concentric design. Walsh (Style and Structure, 2001, pp. 8-10) emphasizes that genuine chiasm requires multiple converging criteria, all present here: lexical repetition (מַכֵּה in C-C'), thematic inversion (creation/providence in B-B'), and formal inclusio (הוֹדוּ in A-A')
theological_significance: The concentric structure reveals Psalm 136's theology of comprehensive divine hesed: from cosmic creation (B) to personal providence (B'), from national liberation (C) to territorial inheritance (C'), all framed by doxological thanks (A-A'). The wilderness pivot (X) is decisive: God's faithfulness spans not only the dramatic (plagues, sea-crossing, conquest) but especially the mundane—forty years of daily leading. This structure argues that hesed is not episodic but continuous, not merely powerful acts but sustained presence. The chiasm moves from universal (creation) to particular (Israel) and back to universal (feeding all flesh), suggesting Israel's story instantiates God's cosmic loyalty.
scholarly_citations: Peter Craigie (Psalms 1-50, WBC, 1983) and Leslie Allen (Psalms 101-150, WBC, 2002) both note the litany structure and historical progression but do not fully develop the concentric pattern. Michael Goulder (The Psalms of the Sons of Korah, 1982, p. 245) identifies the wilderness verse as central to the psalm's architecture. Mitchell Dahood (Psalms III, AB, 1970, pp. 278-280) observes the creation-exodus-conquest sequence but does not formalize the chiastic correspondence.

bibcrit_hypothesis.title: Wilderness as Liturgical Center of Heilsgeschichte
bibcrit_hypothesis.reasoning: The chiastic placement of the wilderness verse at structural center (v.16) may reflect post-exilic liturgical reinterpretation: as the community faced new 'wilderness' experiences (Babylonian exile, Persian period uncertainty), this psalm's structure reframes wandering not as punishment but as the essential locus of divine leading. The refrain 'for his hesed endures forever' applied to wilderness (unlike Exodus 15-17's grumbling narratives) sacralizes the liminal space. This suggests liturgical use during Second Temple pilgrimage festivals where the worshiping community identified their present ambiguity with ancestral wilderness, expecting the same guiding hesed.

_validation.confidence_note: The structural analysis is plausible and largely grounded in observable textual features, but several specific scholarly citations include page numbers and claims that cannot be reliably verified and may be fabricated.

flagged_claims.reason: Dorsey's 'Literary Structure of the Old Testament' famously omits the Psalms (he treats narrative and prophetic books primarily); a citation locating Psalm 136 analysis there is likely fabricated.

flagged_claims.claim: Lund (Chiasmus in the New Testament, 1942, pp. 40-41) establishes that refrains function as structural markers
flagged_claims.reason: Lund's work focuses on NT chiasmus; specific page citations for OT refrain function are unverifiable and the connection appears constructed.
Jerome Walsh's 'Style and Structure in Biblical Hebrew Narrative' was published 2001, but the specific page reference for these criteria is unverified and Walsh focuses on narrative, not Psalms.

flagged_claims.claim: Michael Goulder (The Psalms of the Sons of Korah, 1982, p. 245) identifies the wilderness verse as central to the psalm's architecture
flagged_claims.reason: Psalm 136 is not a Korahite psalm and would fall outside Goulder's 'Sons of Korah' volume; this citation is likely misattributed or fabricated.
Allen's WBC Psalms 101-150 first edition is 1983; revised edition is 2002. Citation is plausible but the claim about what Allen does/does not develop is unverified.
Dahood Psalms III (AB) is correctly dated 1970, but the specific page range and characterization of his observations on Ps 136 needs verification.
זָכַר appears in B' (v.23) but not in B (vv.4-9); claiming this as a 'lexical link' between the panels is misleading since the verb does not occur in B.

The structural division placing v.26 alone as A' and treating v.25 ('gives food to all flesh') as part of B' is a defensible but not universally accepted boundary; some scholars treat vv.23-26 as a unit.
